entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Doing something you are good at and enjoy, so that you feel comfortable, confident and happy.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and profiles, usually with *be* or *look*: *She was in her element at the party.* The possessive matches the subject (*in his / her / their element*). The opposite, *out of your element*, means uncomfortable in an unfamiliar situation.
examples: Put my dad in front of a grill with twenty hungry guests, and he's **in his element**.
The new nurse looked nervous at first, but in the emergency room she was clearly **in her element**.
As a former teacher, Raj was **in his element** explaining the dinosaur bones to a group of kids at the museum.

drill.sentence: Aunt Rosa loves organizing big family dinners; give her a crowd to feed and she's {{in her element}}.
drill.hint: doing what she does best and loving it (not *in her happy place* or *in heaven*)

entries.related: *out of your element* — uncomfortable in an unfamiliar situation; *in your comfort zone* — in a familiar, safe situation; *a natural* — someone who is naturally good at something.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of success, praise or power: to make someone too proud and self-important.
entries.usage: The subject is the success, not the person: *Fame went to his head.* Typical subjects are *success, fame, money, power* and *praise*, and the warning *Don't let it go to your head* is very common. The same phrase is also used about alcohol that makes you dizzy quickly: *The wine went straight to my head.*
entries.pattern: success / fame / power + go to someone's head
examples: After his song went viral, the fame **went to his head**, and he stopped returning his old friends' calls.
Congratulations on the promotion, but don't let it **go to your head**.
The team's early success **went to their heads**, and they lost to the worst team in the league.

drill.sentence: Ever since Ben became captain, the power has {{gone to his head}}; he even tells the coach what to do.
drill.hint: made him arrogant and self-important (not *inflated his ego*)

entries.related: *get a big head* — become arrogant; *full of yourself* — too proud of yourself; *keep your feet on the ground* — stay modest despite success.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To take revenge on someone for something bad they did to you, so that you feel things are equal again.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, films and sports talk: *I'll get even with him.* It often suggests a personal, sometimes petty revenge, and it can be playful between friends or siblings. *Get even* also works without an object: *Don't get mad, get even.*
entries.pattern: get even (with someone) (for something)
examples: My brother ate my birthday cake, so I **got even with him** by hiding his car keys.
After losing the final to them last year, the team was desperate to **get even**.
She felt her boss had humiliated her, but she knew that trying to **get even with** him would only cost her the job.

drill.sentence: My roommate pranked me on April Fools' Day, and I've spent all year planning how to {{get even with}} her.
drill.hint: pay her back for it (not *get back at* or *take revenge on*)

entries.related: *get back at someone* — same meaning; *pay someone back* — punish someone for what they did; *settle a score* — take revenge for an old wrong.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To continue until the end of something long or difficult, without giving up.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business and relationships: *Can this team go the distance?* In boxing it means lasting all the scheduled rounds, and in baseball a pitcher who *goes the distance* pitches the whole game. It is positive and often appears with *can*, *will* or *didn't*.
examples: Nobody thought their marriage would **go the distance**, but they just celebrated their fortieth anniversary.
The starting pitcher **went the distance**, throwing all nine innings.
Lots of people sign up for night classes, but only a few **go the distance** and finish the degree.

drill.sentence: Most people who start the thirty-day fitness challenge quit after a week, but my mom {{went the distance}}.
drill.hint: kept going until the very end (not *saw it through* or *stuck it out*)

entries.related: *see something through* — continue until it is finished; *stick it out* — continue despite difficulty; *throw in the towel* — give up, also from boxing.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Disorganized and without order or focus, or spread out in many different places.
entries.usage: Very common in both American and British English. It has a literal sense (*toys all over the place*) and a critical one about thinking, work or results: *The movie was all over the place.* About a person, *I'm all over the place today* means scattered or emotionally unsettled.
examples: There were toys and wrapping paper **all over the place** after my nephew's birthday party.
The movie was **all over the place**; I still can't tell if it was supposed to be a comedy.
I've had so little sleep that I'm **all over the place** today; I've lost my keys twice.

drill.sentence: My notes from the lecture are {{all over the place}}; I can't find anything I need for the exam.
drill.hint: completely disorganized (not *a mess* or *… the map*)

entries.related: *all over the map* — American, same critical sense; *scattered* — unfocused; *everywhere* — the plain literal word.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To try every possible way to find something or solve a problem.
entries.usage: Used in news, formal promises and determined statements, often by police, officials, lawyers and companies: *We will leave no stone unturned.* It sounds serious and determined, and in official statements it can sound like a cliché. The form is almost always fixed with *no*.
examples: Police say they'll **leave no stone unturned** until they find the missing hiker.
When planning her wedding, my sister **left no stone unturned**; she visited thirty venues.
Health officials **left no stone unturned** in their search for the source of the outbreak.

drill.sentence: Mom {{left no stone unturned}} looking for a doctor who could finally explain my brother's headaches.
drill.hint: tried every possible way — a rock image (not *searched high and low*)

entries.related: *search high and low* — look everywhere; *go to great lengths* — make a big effort; *turn the place upside down* — search a room or house very thoroughly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be in a state where the result is still uncertain, and something important could be won or lost.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and dramatic writing, with serious things as the subject: *lives, jobs, the future, the outcome*. It sounds serious and suspenseful. A typical frame is *with something hanging in the balance*.
entries.pattern: something hangs in the balance / with something hanging in the balance
examples: Hundreds of jobs **hang in the balance** while the company looks for a buyer.
With the game **hanging in the balance**, the coach sent in a rookie to take the final shot.
For two days after the accident, his life **hung in the balance**.

drill.sentence: The town's only hospital may close, and the city council votes tonight; its future {{hangs in the balance}}.
drill.hint: is completely undecided — a weighing image (not *is up in the air* or *is at stake*)

entries.related: *up in the air* — not yet decided, less dramatic; *at stake* — at risk of being lost; *touch and go* — uncertain, especially about survival.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do something new that has never been done before, or to make new discoveries.
entries.usage: Common in news, reviews, science and the arts, almost always admiring: *The album broke new ground.* The adjective *groundbreaking* is related and very common. Don't confuse it with *break ground*, which means to start building something.
examples: Her first novel **broke new ground** by telling a war story from a dog's point of view.
The surgeons **broke new ground** when they gave a ten-year-old boy a new pair of hands.
If you want to **break new ground** in your field, start by reading what's already been done.

drill.sentence: The architect {{broke new ground}} with a museum built entirely from old shipping containers.
drill.hint: did something never done before (not *made history*, *pushed the envelope* or *blazed a trail*)

entries.related: *groundbreaking* — the adjective; *pioneer* — be the first to do something; *break ground* — start building, literally.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A face that shows no emotion, so that other people cannot tell what you are thinking or feeling.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about hiding reactions, typically in *keep a poker face* and *have a good / terrible poker face*. It can be neutral or admiring, and people often joke about their own bad poker face.
entries.pattern: keep a poker face / have a good (terrible) poker face
examples: I tried to keep **a poker face** while my friend showed me her awful new tattoo.
Our accountant has a perfect **poker face**; you never know if the numbers are good or bad until she speaks.
I have a terrible **poker face**, so my kids always know when I'm planning a surprise.

drill.sentence: The judges on the cooking show kept {{a poker face}} while they tasted, so none of the contestants knew who had won.
drill.hint: showed no emotion at all — a card-game image (not *a straight …*)

entries.related: *keep a straight face* — not laugh when something is funny; *deadpan* — showing no emotion, especially in humor; *stone-faced* — serious and unfriendly.
entries.origin: From the card game poker, where players hide any reaction to their cards.

entries.term: hold up your end of the bargain
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do your part of an agreement, as you promised.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, parenting, business and relationships, often as a reminder or a complaint: *I did my part; now hold up your end of the bargain.* The possessive matches the subject. *Keep your end of the bargain* and *uphold your end of the bargain* are common variants.
entries.pattern: hold up / keep your end of the bargain
examples: I cooked dinner, so you have to **hold up your end of the bargain** and do the dishes.
My sister promised to walk the dog every day if we got one, but she hasn't **held up her end of the bargain**.
The landlord fixed the heating, so we **held up our end of the bargain** and signed for another year.

drill.sentence: We let our teenager borrow the car on the condition that he'd wash it every weekend, and so far he's {{held up his end of the bargain}}.
drill.hint: done what he promised in the deal (not *kept …* or *done his part*)

entries.related: *keep your word* — do what you promised; *do your part* — contribute what is expected; *go back on a deal* — fail to do what you agreed.

entries.term: at the top of your game
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Performing at your very best, better than at any other time in your career or activity.
entries.usage: Common in sports and career talk: *She was at the top of her game when she retired.* The possessive matches the subject (*his / her / their game*). It is admiring and used for any skilled work, not just sports; *on top of your game* is a common variant.
examples: She retired from tennis while she was still **at the top of her game**.
After forty years in court, the old lawyer was still **at the top of his game**, calm and sharp.
You need to be **at the top of your game** for an interview at a company like that.

drill.sentence: The chef was {{at the top of his game}} that night; every dish that came out of the kitchen was perfect.
drill.hint: performing at his very finest (not *at his best* or *in top form*)

entries.related: *in top form* — playing or working very well; *at your peak* — at the highest point; *past your prime* — no longer at your best.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Very quickly and by large amounts, about growth, progress or improvement.
entries.usage: Used with verbs like *grow, improve, increase* and *advance*: *Her English has improved by leaps and bounds.* It is positive and fits both speech and writing. *In leaps and bounds* is a common variant with the same meaning.
entries.pattern: grow / improve / increase + by leaps and bounds
examples: My son's reading has improved **by leaps and bounds** since he started going to the library every week.
Interest in pickleball has grown **by leaps and bounds**; our park just added six new courts.
Battery technology has advanced **by leaps and bounds** in the last ten years.

drill.sentence: Ticket sales for the little film festival have increased {{by leaps and bounds}}; this year it moved to a bigger theater.
drill.hint: very fast and by a lot (not *dramatically*)

entries.related: *in leaps and bounds* — a common variant; *by a wide margin* — by a large amount; *at a snail's pace* — the opposite, very slowly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To show what you are really like, especially when this is worse than people believed.
entries.usage: Usually negative: someone who seemed nice turns out to be selfish or dishonest, often under pressure or when money is involved. It is occasionally positive, when a crisis reveals someone's strength. The possessive matches the subject (*showed his true colors*), and American spelling is *colors*.
examples: When he refused to help after the car accident, our neighbor finally **showed his true colors**.
Money has a way of making people **show their true colors**; just watch a family fight over an inheritance.
In the crisis, the new manager **showed her true colors**: calm, fair and the first one in every morning.

drill.sentence: Jake seemed sweet at first, but he {{showed his true colors}} when he yelled at the waiter over a cold coffee.
drill.hint: revealed what he was really like (not *let the mask slip*)

entries.related: *let the mask slip* — accidentally reveal your real character; *show your hand* — reveal your plans; *a wolf in sheep's clothing* — a dangerous person who seems harmless.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Thinking in the same way as someone, so that you understand each other easily.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, about friends, couples and colleagues: *We're on the same wavelength.* It is used with *be* or *seem*, followed by *as* or *with* + person. The negative describes people who keep misunderstanding each other.
entries.pattern: be on the same wavelength (as / with someone)
examples: My business partner and I are **on the same wavelength**; we often finish each other's sentences.
We laughed at the same weird joke in the first five minutes and knew we were **on the same wavelength**.
The new drummer just isn't **on the same wavelength** as the rest of the band.

drill.sentence: My sister and I didn't even need to talk while we cooked; we were completely {{on the same wavelength}}.
drill.hint: thinking exactly alike — a radio image (not *in sync* or *on the … page*)

entries.related: *on the same page* — agreeing about facts or plans, common at work; *in sync* — working together smoothly; *click* — get along well right away.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A large and important part of what you need to do to succeed, often the hardest part.
entries.usage: Usually in *X is half the battle*, where X is a first step such as showing up, starting or understanding the problem: *Knowing what's wrong is half the battle.* It is encouraging and common in advice, coaching and self-help.
entries.pattern: X is half the battle / that's half the battle
examples: With small kids, getting everyone out the door on time is **half the battle**.
"I finally signed up for the gym." "Great, that's **half the battle**."
In a job search, knowing someone inside the company is often more than **half the battle**.

drill.sentence: When you're learning to cook, having sharp knives and a clean kitchen is {{half the battle}}.
drill.hint: a big part of success, often the hardest part — a war image (not *the key*)

entries.related: *the hardest part* — plainer; *a step in the right direction* — some progress; *the first step is the hardest* — starting is the most difficult part.

entries.term: take it to the next level
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To improve something, such as a skill, a business or a performance, so that it reaches a clearly higher standard.
entries.usage: Very common and informal in sports, business and marketing talk; because ads and corporate speech overuse it, it can sound like a cliché. The object varies: *take your cooking / the team / your business to the next level*.
entries.pattern: take something to the next level
examples: If you want to **take** your cooking **to the next level**, buy a good knife and learn to use it.
The team has talent, but they need a real leader to **take it to the next level**.
A few string lights and a fire pit **took** our backyard **to the next level**.

drill.sentence: My grandmother's chili was already great, but a square of dark chocolate {{took it to the next level}}.
drill.hint: made it much better — a video-game image (not *kicked it up a notch*)

entries.related: *kick it up a notch* — informal, make something more exciting or better; *raise the bar* — set a higher standard; *step up your game* — start performing better.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be serious and determined about what you intend to do, so that others should take you seriously.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, sports and news: *The new manager means business.* It usually describes someone showing firm intentions through actions or appearance, sometimes as a warning. The form is fixed and usually in the simple present or past: *You could tell she meant business.*
examples: When Mom uses our full names, we know she **means business**.
The new building manager **means business**: any bike left in the hallway gets removed the same day.
The city **meant business** about the new parking rules; my car was towed within ten minutes.

drill.sentence: The sign on the gate said "Keep Out," and the two big dogs behind it showed that the owner {{meant business}}.
drill.hint: was serious and ready to act (not *wasn't kidding*)

entries.related: *be dead serious* — be completely serious; *put your foot down* — firmly refuse to allow something; *all talk* — the opposite, saying things without acting.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To understand someone's thoughts and feelings very easily, often just from their face or behavior.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, often about family, partners and close friends: *My mom can read me like a book.* It implies that the person cannot hide anything. A person who hides nothing is *an open book*.
entries.pattern: (can) read someone like a book
examples: Don't bother lying to Grandma; she **reads you like a book**.
The detective **read the suspect like a book** and knew right away that he was hiding something.
My best friend took one look at me and **read me like a book**: "You didn't get the job, did you?"

drill.sentence: I tried to act excited about the gift, but my wife {{read me like a book}} and quietly asked if I wanted the receipt.
drill.hint: knew exactly what I was really thinking (not *saw right through me*)

entries.related: *see right through someone* — recognize their lies or real intentions; *an open book* — a person who hides nothing; *read between the lines* — understand a hidden meaning.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be successful in the end after other people doubted, criticized or laughed at you.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business and personal stories, with a satisfied, slightly triumphant tone: *They mocked his idea, but he had the last laugh.* *Get the last laugh* is equally common. The question *Who's laughing now?* expresses the same feeling.
examples: Everyone laughed when Grandpa bought farmland on the edge of town, but he **had the last laugh** when the city grew out to it.
Critics called the movie a flop, but the director **had the last laugh** when it became a cult classic.
Our team was picked to finish last, so winning the league meant we **got the last laugh**.

drill.sentence: My friends teased me for packing an umbrella on a sunny day, but I {{had the last laugh}} when the storm hit.
drill.hint: turned out to be right in the end (not *proved them wrong*)

entries.related: *prove someone wrong* — show that their doubts were mistaken; *Who's laughing now?* — a triumphant question; *he who laughs last laughs best* — the proverb.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of hidden facts or information: to become known, often after a long time.
entries.usage: Common in news and formal writing, especially about wrongdoing, secrets and discoveries: *New evidence has come to light.* The subject is the fact or information, not the person who finds it, and the phrase takes no object. To make something known, use *bring something to light*.
entries.pattern: facts / evidence / details + come to light
examples: New details about the robbery **came to light** after a neighbor shared her doorbell camera footage.
Years later, it **came to light** that my grandfather had a first wife in Ohio.
Old letters that **came to light** during the renovation showed who had built the house.

drill.sentence: The scandal only {{came to light}} when a former employee spoke to reporters.
drill.hint: became known to the public (not *… out*, *surfaced* or *emerged*)

mistake.wrong: The truth finally came to the light.
mistake.right: The truth finally came to light.
mistake.why: The idiom has no article, although German (*ans Licht kommen*) and several other languages use one here.

entries.related: *bring something to light* — reveal it; *come out* — become known, more informal; *surface* — appear after being hidden.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To fight or try very hard, using every possible effort, to get or keep something.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports, business and family stories, often about resisting something: *The company fought tooth and nail to keep its biggest client.* It suggests fierce, sometimes desperate effort. *Tooth and nail* also works with other verbs, such as *battle* or *defend*.
entries.pattern: fight tooth and nail (for / against / to + verb)
examples: Residents **fought tooth and nail** to save the old movie theater from being torn down.
The two brothers **fought tooth and nail** over their mother's house after she died.
My grandmother **fought tooth and nail** against the hospital's plan to send her to a nursing home.

drill.sentence: The nurses {{fought tooth and nail}} for a fair contract and finally got a ten percent raise.
drill.hint: struggled as hard as they could — a biting-and-scratching image (not *… like crazy*)

entries.related: *go to the mat* — fight hard for something, American; *put up a fight* — resist; *fight like cats and dogs* — argue all the time.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A friend who is there when things are going well but disappears when you have problems.
entries.usage: Critical and common in conversation and advice about friendship: *It turns out he was just a fair-weather friend.* *Fair-weather* is written with a hyphen. The pattern extends to supporters: *a fair-weather fan* supports a team only when it wins.
examples: When I lost my job, I found out who my **fair-weather friends** were; half of them stopped calling.
Don't be **a fair-weather friend**; call her now, when she really needs you.
Kayla thought Marcus was **a fair-weather friend**, but he drove six hours to help her move after her divorce.

drill.sentence: Once my brother stopped throwing big parties, his crowd of {{fair-weather friends}} suddenly had other plans every weekend.
drill.hint: pals who are only around in good times (not the *fake* or *so-called* kind)

entries.related: *a true friend* — the opposite; *a friend in need is a friend indeed* — the proverb; *a fair-weather fan* — supports a team only when it wins.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To try to make the best possible impression by showing your best qualities and making a strong effort.
entries.usage: Common in advice about job interviews, first dates, meetings and new jobs: *Put your best foot forward.* It is encouraging, and the possessive matches the subject. *Foot* stays singular, even with *our* or *their*.
examples: It's your first day at the new school, so **put your best foot forward** and smile at people.
We cleaned the whole house and baked bread before the buyers came, trying to **put our best foot forward**.
On a first date, most people **put their best foot forward**, so it takes time to see the real person.

drill.sentence: Wear your nicest suit and get there early; at a job interview you want to {{put your best foot forward}}.
drill.hint: show yourself at your finest (not *make a good impression*)

entries.related: *make a good impression* — plainer; *dress to impress* — dress well to impress others; *look your best* — about appearance only.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A plan or strategy for achieving something, especially one worked out in advance.
entries.usage: Common at work, in sports and in everyday life; it sounds informal and practical. Typical verbs are *have, come up with, stick to* and *change*, and *What's the game plan?* is a common casual question about the next steps.
entries.pattern: have / come up with / stick to a game plan
examples: Before we talk to the bank about a loan, let's agree on **a game plan**.
The coach's **game plan** was simple: slow the game down and keep the ball away from their star.
"So what's the **game plan** for Thanksgiving?" "Turkey at our place, then dessert at Mom's."

drill.sentence: Moving across the country with three kids and a dog takes {{a game plan}}, not just a big truck.
drill.hint: a clear strategy worked out ahead — a sports term (not *a strategy*)

entries.related: *a strategy* — more formal; *a road map* — a step-by-step plan; *wing it* — the opposite, act without a plan.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To an excessive degree, so that a good quality starts to become a problem.
entries.usage: It follows an adjective for a good quality: *generous to a fault*, *honest to a fault*, *loyal to a fault*. It usually sounds affectionate rather than critical, a gentle way to say that someone overdoes a virtue.
entries.pattern: positive adjective + to a fault
examples: My uncle is generous **to a fault**; he once lent his car to a stranger at a gas station.
She's honest **to a fault**, so don't ask her opinion of your haircut unless you really want to know.
Our old family dog was loyal **to a fault**; he wouldn't let the mail carrier near the porch.

drill.sentence: Tom is polite {{to a fault}}; he once apologized to a chair after bumping into it.
drill.hint: excessively, so that a good trait becomes a problem (not *to the extreme*)

mistake.why: *To a fault* follows a positive quality that someone has too much of; with a negative quality, use *extremely* or *very*.

entries.related: *too much of a good thing* — something good that becomes harmful in excess; *to the extreme* — to a very high degree; *overly* — too, as in *overly cautious*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An unfair and hurtful remark or action, especially one that attacks someone's weak point.
entries.usage: Informal and common in arguments and in sports or business commentary: *That was a low blow.* It is often an immediate reaction to something just said, and it can describe actions too, such as a dirty trick by a competitor.
examples: Bringing up my divorce in front of my kids was **a low blow**, even for you.
Posting fake reviews about a competitor is **a low blow**, and customers usually see right through it.
"At least I didn't fail my driving test three times." "Wow, that's **a low blow**."

drill.sentence: Calling me cheap in front of my in-laws was {{a low blow}}, and you know it.
drill.hint: an unfair, hurtful attack (not *a cheap shot* or *below the belt*)

entries.related: *below the belt* — unfair, the same boxing image; *a cheap shot* — an unfair attack, often verbal; *hit someone where it hurts* — attack their weakest point.
entries.origin: From boxing, where hitting an opponent below the belt is against the rules.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Certain to be won or achieved, as if the result were already secured.
entries.usage: Informal and common in sports, business and everyday talk: *The job is in the bag.* It also appears as *have something in the bag* and in warnings: *Don't think it's in the bag yet.* Said too early, it can sound overconfident.
entries.pattern: be in the bag / have something in the bag
examples: We were up by twenty points at halftime, so we thought the game was **in the bag**.
The deal isn't **in the bag** until both sides sign, so don't celebrate yet.
My mom says the blue ribbon for her apple pie is **in the bag** this year.

drill.sentence: Lisa had practiced parallel parking for weeks, so she was sure her driving test was {{in the bag}}.
drill.hint: certain to be passed (not *a sure thing*, *a done deal* or *a slam dunk*)

entries.related: *a sure thing* — something certain to happen; *a done deal* — already agreed or decided; *a slam dunk* — American, something certain to succeed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be in charge of an activity, organization or group and make the important decisions.
entries.usage: Informal, used at work, in families and in organizations: *Who's running the show here?* It is often said about the real decision-maker, who may not be the official boss. It can sound admiring or a little critical.
examples: The owner is rarely there anymore; his daughter **runs the show** at the hardware store now.
Let's be honest: at our house, the cat **runs the show**.
When the director got sick, her assistant **ran the show** for the whole festival.

drill.sentence: The principal has the title, but everyone at the school knows her assistant is the one who {{runs the show}}.
drill.hint: makes all the decisions — a theater image (not *calls the shots*)

entries.related: *call the shots* — make the decisions; *be in charge* — plainer; *wear the pants* — informal, be the dominant partner in a relationship.

entries.term: the pot calling the kettle black
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Said when someone criticizes another person for a fault that they have themselves.
entries.usage: Informal, used in conversation and opinion writing, usually as a reply: *That's the pot calling the kettle black.* It points out hypocrisy, often with humor. *Talk about the pot calling the kettle black* is a common frame.
entries.pattern: That's / Talk about the pot calling the kettle black
examples: My brother, who's never on time, complained that I was late. Talk about **the pot calling the kettle black**.
"You spend way too much time on your phone." "That's **the pot calling the kettle black**, Dad."
When the messiest guy in the office complained about the dirty kitchen, it was **the pot calling the kettle black**.

drill.sentence: Mom criticized my aunt for gossiping, which was a bit like {{the pot calling the kettle black}}, since Mom loves gossip more than anyone.
drill.hint: accusing someone of your own fault — a kitchen image

entries.related: *look who's talking* — informal, same idea; *people who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones* — don't criticize others for your own faults; *hypocritical* — the adjective.

entries.term: air your dirty laundry in public
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To discuss private problems or family arguments in front of other people, often in an embarrassing way.
entries.usage: Critical and common in conversation and news about families, couples, companies and sports teams. The possessive changes, and *in public* is often dropped: *They aired their dirty laundry on social media.* British English also says *wash your dirty linen in public*.
entries.pattern: air your dirty laundry (in public)
examples: My parents never fought in front of guests; they didn't believe in **airing their dirty laundry in public**.
After the breakup, the band **aired its dirty laundry** in a series of angry posts.
Can we please not **air our dirty laundry** in front of the waiter?

drill.sentence: The team's owner and its head coach kept criticizing each other at press conferences, {{airing their dirty laundry}} for the whole league to see.
drill.hint: exposing private disputes publicly — a washing image (not *washing …*)

entries.related: *wash your dirty linen in public* — the British version; *keep it in the family* — the opposite; *a family feud* — a long argument within a family.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be a normal and expected part of a job, role or situation, even if it is unpleasant.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and interviews, usually to accept a downside calmly: *Long hours come with the territory.* The subject is the downside, and *go with the territory* means the same. It sounds realistic and slightly resigned.
entries.pattern: a downside + comes with the territory
examples: Being recognized at the grocery store **comes with the territory** when you read the local news on TV.
Sleepless nights **come with the territory** when you have a newborn.
Angry parents **come with the territory** if you coach a high school football team in Texas.

drill.sentence: Sand in the car and the occasional sunburn {{come with the territory}} when you live two blocks from the beach.
drill.hint: are a normal, expected part of it (not *are part of the deal* or *are par for the course*)

entries.related: *go with the territory* — same meaning; *part and parcel of* — an essential part of; *par for the course* — normal and expected, usually about something bad.

entries.term: someone's heart is in the right place
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Someone has good intentions and means well, even if what they do goes wrong or annoys people.
entries.usage: Used to defend or excuse someone kindly, often next to *but*: *He's clumsy, but his heart is in the right place.* The possessive changes (*her heart*, *their hearts*). It sounds warm and forgiving.
entries.pattern: …, but his / her / their heart(s) is / are in the right place
examples: My uncle's gifts are always a little strange, but **his heart is in the right place**.
The new volunteers made a mess of the food drive, but **their hearts were in the right place**.
**Her heart is in the right place**; she just doesn't know when to stop giving advice.

drill.sentence: Grandpa tried to fix my bike and broke the chain, but {{his heart was in the right place}}.
drill.hint: he had good intentions (not *he meant well*)

entries.related: *mean well* — have good intentions; *well-meaning* — the adjective; *with the best of intentions* — meaning well, though things go wrong.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The stressful, competitive and tiring life of modern work, where people struggle for money and success.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and writing about work and lifestyle, almost always critical or weary. Typical phrases are *escape / get out of the rat race* and *be stuck in the rat race*. It describes a whole way of life, not one job.
entries.pattern: escape / quit / be stuck in the rat race
examples: After twenty years in finance, he quit **the rat race** and opened a surf shop in Hawaii.
Commuting two hours a day to pay for a house I barely see? I'm tired of **the rat race**.
Many young families move to small towns hoping to escape **the rat race**.

drill.sentence: My parents sold their house in the city, bought a farm in Vermont and left {{the rat race}} behind for good.
drill.hint: the exhausting competition of working life (not *the daily grind*)

entries.related: *the daily grind* — boring daily work, without the idea of competition; *dog-eat-dog* — very competitive; *the nine-to-five* — an ordinary office job.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To move up to higher and better-paid positions in a company, step by step.
entries.usage: Neutral to slightly critical, common in talk about careers and ambition: *She spent twenty years climbing the corporate ladder.* It often suggests effort, competition and sometimes sacrifice. *Climb the ladder* alone is also used.
examples: She spent fifteen years **climbing the corporate ladder** before becoming the bank's first female CEO.
My dad never wanted to **climb the corporate ladder**; he was happy fixing machines on the factory floor.
Some people **climb the corporate ladder** quickly by changing companies every two years.

drill.sentence: Instead of {{climbing the corporate ladder}} at a big firm, Diego decided to open his own bike repair shop.
drill.hint: working his way up through the ranks of a company (not *moving up*)

entries.related: *move up the ranks* — get promoted; *a career ladder* — the steps of a career; *a dead-end job* — one with no chance of promotion.

entries.term: burn the candle at both ends
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To work or stay busy from early morning until late at night, so that you sleep too little and become exhausted.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and advice, often as a warning: *You can't keep burning the candle at both ends.* It usually describes a period of overwork plus late nights, such as a job combined with classes or a busy social life. It is very often in the progressive.
examples: Between her night classes and her day job, Ana has been **burning the candle at both ends** for months.
If you keep **burning the candle at both ends**, you're going to get sick.
Most accountants **burn the candle at both ends** from February until the April tax deadline.

drill.sentence: He worked double shifts all week and went out dancing every night; no wonder he got sick from {{burning the candle at both ends}}.
drill.hint: too much work and too little sleep — a light image (not *overdoing it* or *running himself ragged*)

entries.related: *run yourself ragged* — exhaust yourself; *work yourself to the bone* — work extremely hard; *pull an all-nighter* — stay up all night working or studying.

entries.term: up to your ears in something
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Having too much of something to deal with, especially work, bills or problems.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation: *I'm up to my ears in paperwork.* The possessive matches the subject, and the thing is usually unpleasant (*work, debt, laundry, emails*). *Up to your neck in* is similar but often means deeply involved in trouble.
entries.pattern: be up to your ears in + noun
examples: I can't take on anything else this month; I'm **up to my ears in** work.
After the twins were born, we were **up to our ears in** diapers and laundry.
Thanks to student loans, lots of college graduates are **up to their ears in** debt.

drill.sentence: My sister can't come to the beach this weekend; she's {{up to her ears in}} wedding planning.
drill.hint: completely overloaded with (not *swamped with* or *buried in*)

entries.related: *up to your neck in* — deeply involved, often in trouble; *swamped* — very busy; *snowed under* — having too much work.

entries.term: keep your eye on the ball
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stay focused on what matters most and not get distracted.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business and advice: *Keep your eye on the ball and don't worry about the competition.* It comes from coaches telling players in baseball, tennis or golf to watch the ball. The possessive changes, and *take your eye off the ball* means to lose focus.
examples: With finals next week, I need to **keep my eye on the ball** and stay off social media.
Our founder reminds us to **keep our eye on the ball**: happy customers, not fancy offices.
Weddings are full of distractions, but **keep your eye on the ball**; the point is marrying someone you love.

drill.sentence: Don't get distracted by all the fancy features; {{keep your eye on the ball}} and buy the car that's safest for the kids.
drill.hint: concentrate on what matters most — a sports image (not *stay focused*)

entries.related: *take your eye off the ball* — lose focus; *stay on track* — continue as planned; *see the big picture* — understand the overall situation.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To talk about your work with people from the same job in a social situation, often boring others who are present.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, often in the negative or as an apology: *Sorry, we're talking shop again.* *Shop* has no article here. The noun is *shop talk* (also *shoptalk*).
examples: Every time my wife gets together with her nurse friends, they end up **talking shop** about patients.
No **talking shop** at dinner, please; it's my birthday.
Sorry, I didn't mean to **talk shop**; you must be bored to tears.

drill.sentence: At the wedding, the three lawyers stood by the bar all night and {{talked shop}} while their partners danced.
drill.hint: discussed their jobs at a social event (not *… business*)

entries.related: *shop talk* — the noun; *talk business* — discuss business matters, often on purpose; *leave work at the office* — not bring work into your private life.

entries.term: put in a good word for someone
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To say something positive about someone to a person with influence, in order to help them get a job, a chance or a favor.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, often as a request or an offer: *Could you put in a good word for me with your manager?* The full frame is *put in a good word for someone (with someone)*. The order *put a good word in for* is also common.
entries.pattern: put in a good word for someone (with someone)
examples: My cousin works at the hospital, and she **put in a good word for** me with the head of nursing.
If you talk to your coach, could you **put in a good word for** my son? He'd love to join the team.
Thanks for **putting in a good word for** me; I got the apartment!

drill.sentence: My neighbor knows the owner of the restaurant, so she offered to {{put in a good word for}} me when I applied to wait tables.
drill.hint: speak favorably about me (not *vouch for* or *recommend*)

entries.related: *vouch for someone* — say that someone is honest or capable, using your own reputation; *recommend* — plainer; *pull strings* — use influence to help someone, often unfairly.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To work hard for a long time, often in low or unpleasant positions, before you earn success or respect.
entries.usage: Common in talk about careers, music, sports and the arts: *She paid her dues in small clubs for years.* It suggests that success was earned, not given. The literal sense (paying membership fees) also exists, so context matters.
examples: Before he became a famous comedian, he **paid his dues** in tiny clubs for ten years.
Medical residents **pay their dues** with long night shifts and weekends on call.
I **paid my dues** washing dishes and peeling potatoes before anyone let me cook.

drill.sentence: The rookie spent two seasons on the bench before he got to start; like everyone, he had to {{pay his dues}}.
drill.hint: put in years of hard, unglamorous work first (not *earn his stripes*)

entries.related: *earn your stripes* — prove yourself through experience; *work your way up* — rise step by step; *start at the bottom* — begin in the lowest position.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Someone who can do many different jobs or tasks reasonably well.
entries.usage: Used about handy people, workers and generalists. On its own it is usually a compliment, but the full saying *a jack of all trades, master of none* is critical: good at many things, excellent at none. People often use it modestly about themselves.
examples: Our building's super is **a jack of all trades**; he fixes leaks, paints walls and even repairs bikes.
At a small startup, you have to be **a jack of all trades**.
I'm **a jack of all trades**, master of none: I play four instruments, all of them badly.

drill.sentence: My grandfather could fix cars, build furniture and cut hair; he was {{a jack of all trades}}.
drill.hint: good at many kinds of work (not *a handyman* or *a Renaissance man*)

entries.related: *a handyman* — someone who does small repairs; *a generalist* — someone with broad rather than deep skills; *a Renaissance man* — someone talented in many fields, more admiring.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: In control of a situation or task, so that you are dealing with it well and are not behind.
entries.usage: Very common at work and in daily life, in *be / stay / keep / get on top of something*, especially with *emails, bills, the schedule* or *things*. *I'm on top of it* is a reassuring reply to a request or a worry.
entries.pattern: be / stay / keep / get on top of something
examples: With three kids and a full-time job, it's hard to stay **on top of** the laundry.
"Did anyone call the plumber?" "Yeah, I'm **on top of** it."
Nurses on the night shift have to stay **on top of** every patient's medication schedule.

drill.sentence: Sorry I missed your email; I'm trying to get back {{on top of}} things after two weeks of vacation.
drill.hint: managing well and not behind (not *in control of*)

entries.related: *in control of* — plainer; *keep up with* — not fall behind; *fall behind* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To find and fix the small problems in a new system, plan or product so that it works smoothly.
entries.usage: Informal American English, common at work and about new routines, products or schedules: *We're still working out the kinks.* It suggests the problems are small and normal at the start. *Iron out the kinks* is a common variant.
entries.pattern: work out / iron out the kinks (in something)
examples: The new online ordering system has a few bugs, but we're still **working out the kinks**.
Our carpool schedule was chaos at first, but we **worked out the kinks** after a couple of weeks.
The restaurant had a soft opening to **work out the kinks** before the big launch.

drill.sentence: The new bus route is a little confusing right now, but the city says it will {{work out the kinks}} by spring.
drill.hint: fix the small early problems (not *iron …*)

entries.related: *iron out the kinks / wrinkles* — same idea; *teething problems* — British, early problems with something new; *growing pains* — problems that come with growth.

entries.term: put your heart and soul into something
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To put a lot of effort, energy and enthusiasm into something because you care about it deeply.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, interviews and tributes: *She put her heart and soul into that school.* It sounds warm and admiring. The possessive matches the subject, and *into* + the activity or project follows.
entries.pattern: put your heart and soul into + noun / -ing
examples: My mom **put her heart and soul into** that garden, and it shows.
The players **put their heart and soul into** every game, even in a losing season.
I **put my heart and soul into** that application, so the rejection really hurt.

drill.sentence: Grandpa spent three years restoring the old fishing boat; he {{put his heart and soul into}} every board.
drill.hint: gave all his love and effort to — a body-and-spirit image (not *poured … into*)

entries.related: *pour your heart into something* — similar; *give it your all* — make the greatest effort; *go through the motions* — the opposite, do something without real effort.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To consider something carefully before doing it, often deciding not to do it.
entries.usage: Very common in speech and writing, often as a warning: *I'd think twice before lending him money.* Typical frames are *think twice before* + -ing, *think twice about* + noun and *make someone think twice*. *Without thinking twice* means immediately, without hesitation.
entries.pattern: think twice before + -ing / about + noun
examples: I'd **think twice** before lending him money; he still owes me from last year.
The huge fine should make drivers **think twice** about texting behind the wheel.
When the neighbors' garage caught fire, my dad ran over to help without **thinking twice**.

drill.sentence: That online deal looks too good to be true; I'd {{think twice}} before giving them my credit card number.
drill.hint: consider it very carefully first (not *hesitate* or *be careful*)

entries.related: *have second thoughts* — begin to doubt a decision; *look before you leap* — the proverb; *sleep on it* — wait a night before deciding.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The boring, tiring routine of work or tasks that you have to do every day.
entries.usage: Informal and common in conversation, with a weary or humorous tone, often in *back to the daily grind* after a vacation or a weekend. It is about routine more than stress, unlike *the rat race*, which stresses competition.
examples: After a week at the beach, it's back to **the daily grind** on Monday.
Between the commute, the meetings and the kids' homework, **the daily grind** wears me out.
Retirement freed my parents from **the daily grind**, and now they travel half the year.

drill.sentence: Coffee with my neighbor every morning is the one thing that makes {{the daily grind}} bearable.
drill.hint: the dull everyday routine of work — a mill image (not *the rat race*)

entries.related: *the rat race* — the competitive side of working life; *the nine-to-five* — an ordinary office job; *a rut* — a dull routine that is hard to escape.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A view from high above, or a general overview of a subject without the details.
entries.usage: Used literally about views from planes, towers and hills (*a bird's-eye view of the city*) and figuratively about summaries (*a bird's-eye view of the market*). It is neutral and fits both conversation and writing. Note the apostrophe and the hyphen in *bird's-eye*.
entries.pattern: a bird's-eye view of + noun
examples: From the top of the Ferris wheel, we got **a bird's-eye view** of the whole fair.
The first chapter gives readers **a bird's-eye view** of the city's history before going into detail.
Our weekly report gives the managers **a bird's-eye view** of every project in the company.

drill.sentence: We took a helicopter tour over the Grand Canyon, which gave us {{a bird's-eye view}} of the river far below.
drill.hint: a look from high above — an animal image (not *an aerial …*)

entries.related: *an aerial view* — a view from the air, more technical; *the big picture* — the overall situation; *an overview* — a general summary.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Being planned, prepared or developed, but not yet finished or announced.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation, news and entertainment reporting: *A sequel is in the works.* British English more often says *in the pipeline*. It signals that something is coming but may not be certain or public yet.
examples: A sequel to the movie is already **in the works**, according to the director.
We have a big family trip to Italy **in the works** for next summer.
There's a new grocery store **in the works** for our neighborhood, but nobody knows when it will open.

drill.sentence: Nothing is official yet, but a new season of the show is {{in the works}}.
drill.hint: being planned and prepared (not *in the pipeline* or *underway*)

entries.related: *in the pipeline* — same, more common in British English; *on the drawing board* — at the early planning stage; *underway* — already started.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To seem honest, accurate and believable.
entries.usage: Used in conversation, reviews and writing about stories, excuses, claims and characters: *Her story rings true.* The subject is the statement or story, not the person. *Doesn't ring true* and *ring hollow* are very common negatives.
examples: His excuse about a flat tire didn't **ring true**; he'd been posting photos from a bar all evening.
The novel's characters **ring true** because the author grew up in that small Ohio town.
Her apology seemed to **ring true**, so I decided to give her another chance.

drill.sentence: The salesman said the car had only one owner, a retired teacher, but something about his story didn't {{ring true}}.
drill.hint: seem honest and believable (not *add up* or *sound right*)

entries.related: *ring hollow* — sound insincere; *add up* — make sense; *have the ring of truth* — seem true, more formal.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Something that is supposed to be secret but that many people already know.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation: *It's an open secret that the coach is leaving.* Typical frames are *It's an open secret that …* and *an open secret in* + a place or group (*in the office*, *in Hollywood*). It often suggests that people pretend not to know.
entries.pattern: It's an open secret that …
examples: It's **an open secret** in our office that the boss is retiring next year.
It was **an open secret** that the star player wanted a trade.
My grandmother's famous "secret" recipe is **an open secret**; it's printed on the back of the soup can.

drill.sentence: Officially, nobody knows about Dad's surprise party, but it's {{an open secret}}; even Dad has heard about it.
drill.hint: something hidden that everyone knows anyway (not *common knowledge* or *the worst-kept …*)

entries.related: *common knowledge* — something everyone knows, with no secrecy; *the worst-kept secret* — a secret almost everyone knows; *the elephant in the room* — an obvious problem nobody mentions.
